stories.headline: Trump proposes new tariffs on major trading partners; China, EU push back

spectrum.tilt_pill: Coverage is balanced across the spectrum

claims.text: The Trump administration proposed new tariffs on goods from 14 major U.S. trading partners, including China, the EU, Japan, South Korea, Vietnam and Cambodia.

Proposed rates include up to 40% on Chinese goods, 35% on Vietnamese goods, and 20-25% on goods from other listed countries, plus additional tariffs on Brazilian sugar and aircraft on top of existing levies.

For most countries the White House listed two possible rates — a higher 'proposed rate' and a lower 'deal rate' (e.g., China's deal rate is 20% versus a proposed 40%) — with the final rate contingent on ongoing negotiations.
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the tariffs could take effect within a couple of months.

The tariffs are being imposed under Section 301 of U.S. trade law, which the administration says targets other countries' 'structural excess capacity' and unfair trade practices such as subsidies, tax breaks and labor practices.
This proposal follows a Supreme Court ruling earlier this year that struck down separate tariffs the administration had imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA).
A lawsuit filed by the Liberty and Justice Center is already challenging earlier Section 301 tariffs, arguing they exceeded what the statute permits.
House Ways and Means Committee ranking Democrat Richard Neal and Senator Tim Kaine (D-Va.) have publicly criticized the new tariff plan.

The new tariff proposal is an attempt by the Trump administration to replace sweeping tariffs that the Supreme Court invalidated, this time relying on a different legal authority — Section 301 — that is meant to counter specific unfair trade practices rather than serve as a broad negotiating tool.

Because the law requires a country-specific justification, trade experts and critics question whether applying it uniformly across 14 partners, with a dual 'proposed' and 'deal' rate structure, fits its intended purpose, setting up likely legal challenges similar to the one already pending against earlier 301 tariffs.
Senator Kaine notes consumer prices, including holiday costs, have risen partly due to tariffs.
Senator Kaine ties recent Democratic warnings to midterm election losses widely attributed to high prices.

Underlying the dispute is a long-standing debate over whether unilateral, broad-based tariffs or allied, coordinated pressure is more effective at addressing practices by countries like China that most policymakers agree involve unfair trade conduct.
Across the debate, there is broad agreement — including from critics like Sen. Kaine — that certain countries, particularly China, engage in trade practices many consider unfair.
The core disagreement is not whether a problem exists but whether broad, unilateral 301 tariffs on allies and rivals alike are the legally sound and strategically effective way to address it.

The proposed tariffs' fate will likely hinge on three unresolved tracks: ongoing trade negotiations that could lower rates to the 'deal' level, pending and possible new legal challenges over whether Section 301 permits such broad application, and congressional efforts — led by Democrats but requiring Republican votes — to curb presidential tariff authority.

Consumers and businesses face continued uncertainty over final rates and potential price effects until these processes resolve, likely within the next couple of months per the administration's stated timeline.

stories.headline: Severe weather disrupts Thanksgiving travel; Macy's parade postponed

claims.text: Macy's postponed its 100th annual Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York City from Thursday to Saturday.
The postponement was due to a powerful nor'easter.
This was the first weather-related postponement in the parade's history.
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul declared a state of emergency for Long Island, New York City and Westchester County.
New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill declared a state of emergency across all 21 of New Jersey's counties.
The National Weather Service issued a high wind warning for the New York area from 10:00 a.m. Thursday to 1:00 a.m. Friday.
The high wind warning included gusts up to 60 mph.
The National Weather Service forecast heavy rain, coastal flooding and inland snow for the New York area.
Record 'king tides' hit California during Thanksgiving week.
Tides reached 8 feet 11 inches in San Diego.
Tides reached 8.19 feet in Los Angeles.
These tides broke records set in late October.
A portion of a pier in northern California collapsed into the ocean.
AAA projected 81.5 million Americans would travel at least 50 miles from home for Thanksgiving between Nov. 24 and Nov. 30.
A flood warning was issued for Vancouver, British Columbia's coastline due to king tides.
Additional storms were forecast for the Pacific Northwest.
NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani said the postponement was necessary due to extreme weather.
Mayor Mamdani confirmed an expanded police presence for Saturday's rescheduled parade.
Mayor Mamdani said he would not attend the rescheduled parade due to a scheduled surgery.
President Trump called for a probe into GDP data, according to The Hill.

One system is a nor'easter moving up the East Coast bringing high winds, heavy rain and coastal flooding.

California and Canadian officials issued flood warnings as tide records were broken for the second time in a month.
The nor'easter and king tides are expected to continue moving through the affected regions into Friday.

stories.headline: Two Italians killed in Kuwait drone strike; Iran denies involvement
body: Two Italian nationals were killed and two other workers wounded on Thursday when falling shrapnel from intercepted Iranian drones struck a vital site in Kuwait, according to Kuwait's Ministry of Defence. The victims were technicians for the German arms manufacturer Rheinmetall Italia, working at an air-defence surveillance station performing maintenance on systems used by the Kuwaiti Armed Forces, Italy's foreign ministry confirmed. The wounded include a Kuwaiti and a Pakistani national.

Kuwait's army said the attack was the result of 'heinous Iranian aggression' and that its forces had detected and intercepted a number of drones from Iran. The two Italians died from their injuries after being hit by falling debris as authorities attempted to shoot down the incoming drones, the defence ministry stated. Italian media identified the deceased as a 36-year-old and a 65-year-old who was nearing retirement.

Iran has strongly denied responsibility. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, in a phone call with his Kuwaiti counterpart Jarrah Jaber Al-Ahmad Al-Sabah, 'firmly rejected allegations regarding an Iranian drone attack on Kuwait, stating that the Islamic Republic of Iran had no involvement whatsoever,' according to state TV. Araghchi offered to conduct a 'joint investigation with the Kuwaiti side' into the incident. Armed forces spokesman Sardar Shekarchi said there had been 'no offensive or military operations in the region' and suggested the accusations were a cover for 'increasing insecurity in the region.'

The attack occurred while the Kuwaiti National Guard and military were meeting with an Italian delegation that included the commander general of the Italian Carabinieri, Lieutenant-General Salvatore Lungo, and the Italian ambassador to Kuwait, according to Al Jazeera's Zein Basravi. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni expressed 'deepest sorrow' and condolences to the victims' families. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called for increased pressure on Iran, stating that 'security in the Gulf is a security issue for us all.'

The incident comes just over a week after Kuwait said it had repelled overnight Iranian drone attacks on an airbase hosting US forces, the first such strikes in more than two months. The broader conflict began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in late February, followed by Iranian missile and drone attacks on Israel and Gulf Arab states hosting US military assets. Gulf states have been caught in the crossfire, with US military facilities and energy installations on their soil targeted. Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi, secretary-general of the Gulf Cooperation Council, condemned the 'brutal' attack, stressing that Iran's continued strikes on Kuwait constitute a dangerous escalation and threaten regional security.

stories.headline: Kushner says Putin showed 'restraint' by not using nuclear weapons, calls Ukraine war a 'proxy' conflict
body: White House envoy Jared Kushner said Russian President Vladimir Putin has "shown restraint" by not using nuclear weapons in the conflict with Ukraine, describing the Russian leader as a "grand man of politics" and a "historic figure." In a wide-ranging interview for Axel Springer CEO Mathias Döpfner's "MD Meets" podcast, Kushner — who is President Donald Trump's son-in-law — said he was convinced Putin wanted peace and a new beginning in relations with the United States. "So far Putin has showed restraint; he's agreed not to use nuclear weapons, which obviously is a big thing, and he's reassured us that that's not his intention," Kushner said.

Kushner and fellow US negotiator Steve Witkoff have met Putin several times, most recently this month at the Kremlin. Kushner said Putin "takes a lot of notes when we're speaking, and he transmits very specifically. But it's very clear he has a very deep understanding of the issues." Kushner rejected suggestions that the US had applied pressure on Ukraine to make concessions to Russia, though Ukraine has said the US Defense Department has delayed shipments of vital air defense missiles and intelligence sharing has been disrupted.

Kushner described the war as a "proxy" conflict, warning that "Europe is funding and arming Ukraine against Russia, and it won't take a lot of miscalculation for this thing to escalate massively." He said Putin opposed a ceasefire because he doubted it would lead to a lasting peace agreement, and that the Russian leader "sees many provocative statements and actions coming from Europe" and "believes that Europe is not ready for peace and instead seeks the strategic defeat of Russia." Kushner's remarks come after several US lawmakers accused him and Witkoff earlier this month of seeking to undermine Ukraine and NATO.

As for efforts to reach a settlement that would include issues of territorial control, Kushner said: "This isn't about fairness or who's right or wrong." Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said earlier this month that US negotiators had floated the idea of Ukraine withdrawing its remaining forces from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for membership of NATO. "The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins Nato? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?' This was the first time this had been raised," Zelensky said after meeting Kushner and Witkoff. Ukraine has long resisted the idea of ceding land to Russia, which launched an unprovoked full-scale invasion in 2022.

Zelensky said if he received a "comprehensive security package" — including a strong Ukrainian army and guarantees from NATO and the European Union — he would put a proposal to the public. Alluding to that possibility, Kushner told Döpfner, "Without a security guarantee from America, Ukraine will not be safe in the future… President Trump has to determine that a security guarantee is in the interests of America to give." Kushner said the ultimate goal was that "if you can end this war in a way where Ukraine is sovereign, secure, prosperous, and free, they could join the EU. They have a post-war economy plan. They have credible security guarantees. They have strong deterrence capabilities. That's a huge victory for Ukraine and for Europe."

stories.headline: Israeli judges recommend dropping most serious charges against Netanyahu
body: Judges in Benjamin Netanyahu's long-running corruption trial recommended on Wednesday that prosecutors drop the most serious case against him, saying the prospects of securing a conviction were low. The recommendation, delivered in a highly unusual hearing at the Jerusalem District Court, could give the caretaker prime minister a boost as he fights for political survival following an inconclusive general election last month.

The judges addressed three cases against Netanyahu, who has been charged since 2019 with bribery, fraud and breach of trust. In Case 4000, which alleges he granted favours to telecommunications company Bezeq in exchange for positive coverage on a news site owned by the company's chair, Judge Rivka Friedman-Feldman told Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara that 'the chances of conviction are low – to an extent that warrants reconsidering the matter,' according to Israeli media. In Case 2000, concerning an alleged deal with Israeli daily Yedioth Ahronoth for favourable coverage, the judges questioned whether the conduct constituted a criminal offence and called for the matter to be reconsidered. In Case 1000, involving accusations that Netanyahu and his wife received gifts and payments from an Australian billionaire in return for political favours, the judges suggested prosecutors and the defence seek an agreement to conclude the proceedings, though a verdict remained an option.

The judges do not have the power to drop charges themselves; their recommendation is directed at Attorney General Baharav-Miara, a longstanding political opponent of Netanyahu who has challenged several government policies. Responding to the court, she said, 'Every statement and proposal raised just now by the court' will be considered, adding, 'We are open to examining everything. Including things that were argued in the past.' She also noted that her office had previously been ready to accept a proposal from Netanyahu's lawyers to conclude proceedings through a deal, saying, 'Our extended hand remains.'

Netanyahu, who has consistently denied the allegations and called the cases a political witch-hunt, said in a televised statement that the 'fabricated cases' against him were falling apart. 'Ten years of terrible suffering for me, my family, my son,' he said. 'Ten years of incitement to hatred that wounds the soul.' He called for the trial to be ended 'immediately' and urged political unity, saying, 'I know what enormous and immediate dangers the state of Israel faces. There is only one way to deal with them. To unite in order to deal with them.' None of Israel's main opposition politicians have yet commented on the judges' advice.

The development comes as Netanyahu's rival Gadi Eisenkot attempts to form a coalition government after last month's election, in which Netanyahu's parliamentary bloc won more seats but both sides fell short of an outright majority. Legal scholar Barak Medina of The Hebrew University of Jerusalem called the judges' intervention 'unprecedented in its nature,' noting that they 'expressed their views before the prosecution had an opportunity to present its arguments.' Netanyahu remains subject to an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza, which he also denies.

stories.headline: Italy rebukes Ukraine for attacks on Russian ships in Mediterranean, citing Libya sovereignty violation
body: Italy has rebuked Ukraine for carrying out attacks against Russian vessels in Libyan waters, saying Kyiv was wrong to violate Libya's sovereignty. The strike, which occurred Sunday night, targeted a Russian warship and a cargo vessel transporting military equipment off Libya's coast, according to Kyiv. Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha described the vessels as legitimate targets, arguing Kyiv had the legal right to defend itself against Russian aggression, and stressed that Ukraine respects Libya's territorial integrity.

The attack on the warship at Benghazi port in eastern Libya killed two naval officers of the self-styled Libyan National Army (LNA), according to Libya's eastern-based forces. Musa al-Koni, vice president of Libya's Tripoli-based Presidential Council, called the attack 'a declaration of war against the Libyan state.' The LNA, which controls eastern and southern parts of Libya and maintains close relations with Russia, promised to retaliate 'at the appropriate time and place, and by the appropriate means.'

Italy's Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani said it was a mistake for Ukraine to violate Libya's sovereignty and that Rome, which has a small military presence in Libya, had received no prior notice of the operation. 'Italy was absolutely unaware of Kyiv's intentions to strike in Libyan territorial waters, even inside a port,' Tajani told Italy's Corriere della Sera newspaper. Italy's far-right League party, a member of the coalition government, also criticized the attack, saying it risked sowing instability inside Libya.

The rebuke marks a rare rift between Italy and Ukraine. Italy has largely supported Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, providing more than 3 billion euros ($3.29bn) in military aid, according to data from the Kiel Institute, and backing sweeping sanctions against Russia. However, there has been division within Italy's government over further aid, with Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini, who heads the League party, opposing more weapons shipments or funding. Matteo Villa, a senior research fellow at the Italian Institute for International Political Studies (ISPI), said the attack off Libya is likely to deepen these domestic tensions, giving Salvini an opportunity to question whether Western military assistance risks enabling Ukraine to pursue objectives that run counter to Italy's own national interests.

Italy's concerns are fueled by its geographical proximity to Libya—its southern islands lie 300km across the Mediterranean from the Libyan coast—as well as its economic and strategic interests there. Last year, Libya accounted for roughly a quarter of Italy's crude oil imports, making it Italy's largest supplier, and the country is the main departure point for migrants reaching Italy by sea. Alessia Melcangi, a nonresident senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, said Italy's condemnation partly serves as 'damage control' to help Rome balance its competing geopolitical interests. 'Rome needs to demonstrate that its relationships with Kyiv, Tripoli and Benghazi give it meaningful influence over developments affecting its security,' she said.

The attacks are part of a broader Ukrainian campaign to strike Russian vessels and infrastructure far from Ukraine. In recent weeks, Ukraine has targeted a Russian cargo vessel off the Finnish coast, a Russian corvette in the Mediterranean, and a dry cargo vessel allegedly carrying weapons off Libya. stories.headline: Fed's preferred inflation gauge accelerated to 3.8% in October, virtually assuring a December rate hike
body: The Federal Reserve's preferred inflation measure accelerated to 3.8% in October, reinforcing expectations that the central bank will raise interest rates at its December meeting and raising questions about how much more tightening may be needed in 2027. The personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, reported Wednesday by the Commerce Department, rose at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.8%, in line with the Dow Jones consensus estimate and nearly double the Fed's 2% target. The reading was 0.1 percentage point higher than September's level.

Excluding volatile food and energy prices, core PCE stood at 3.3%, 0.1 percentage point above forecasts. While the Fed officially follows the headline figure, policymakers consider core to be a more reliable longer-term gauge of inflation trends. Consumer spending rose 0.3% for the month, matching the pace of price increases but falling 0.1 percentage point short of expectations. Personal income surged 0.7%, well above the 0.4% estimate, and the personal saving rate rose to 4.1%.

A separate report showed the U.S. economy grew at a much stronger pace than previously estimated in the third quarter. Gross domestic product rose at a 4.3% annualized rate, according to a revised Commerce Department estimate, driven by upward revisions to investment, consumer spending, and government spending. Consumer spending, which accounts for about two-thirds of economic activity, increased 4.2% in the quarter. A metric known as real final sales to private domestic purchasers — which Fed officials regard as a key indicator of underlying demand — jumped 5.8%, reflecting an upward revision of 0.9 percentage point.

"Inflation is too hot and it will not be brought under control as long as economic demand is also too hot," said Chris Rupkey, chief economist at Fwdbonds. The strong GDP reading adds to the notion that Fed monetary policy is not yet restricting economic activity. Inflation has been running above target for some 5½ years. It had been drifting lower but spiked again following the late-February attacks on Iran led by the U.S. and Israel. Tariffs have continued to exert pressure, as has strong demand associated with the artificial intelligence buildout. The White House on Wednesday announced a fresh round of tariffs on 14 trading partners including China, the European Union, and Japan.

The market is fully pricing in a quarter-percentage-point interest rate hike when the Fed meets Dec. 8-9. Less certain is how much more rates will need to increase to get inflation back to 2%. Traders continued to price in two more rate increases in 2027 but lowered odds for a third hike to about 1-in-3, compared to 50-50 on Tuesday, according to the CME Group's FedWatch. Stock market futures added to losses following the release, while Treasury yields were sharply lower.

In other economic news Wednesday, the Labor Department reported that initial jobless claims fell to 189,000 for the week ending Nov. 21, down 13,000 from the prior week and back to around the lowest level since the late 1960s. Wall Street had expected 200,000.

stories.headline: Spain's Pablo Hernández de Cos set to lead European Central Bank
body: Pablo Hernández de Cos is set to become the next president of the European Central Bank, succeeding Christine Lagarde when she steps down on Feb. 7, 2027. Euro zone leaders backed the Spanish economist at the European Council Summit, according to multiple media reports on Thursday, after the Netherlands agreed to support Klaas Knot, the only other candidate. The formal appointment still requires consultation with the European Parliament and the ECB's Governing Council, though neither body has veto power over the eight-year term.

De Cos, 55, is a career central banker who rose through the ranks of the Bank of Spain, starting as a researcher in the 1990s and serving as its governor from 2018 to June 2024. He chaired the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision from 2019 to 2024 and has been General Manager of the Bank for International Settlements since July 2025. Analysts describe him as moderately dovish but pragmatic, willing to support strong rate hikes during the energy price shock after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, while also backing the negative rates and stimulus package launched by then-ECB President Mario Draghi in 2019. De Cos has called himself an "owl" focused on data and the situation at hand, rather than a hawk or dove.

The appointment follows intense political horse-trading among the euro area's largest economies — Germany, France, Italy, Spain and the Netherlands — as they jockeyed for influence on the ECB's six-member Executive Board. Alongside de Cos as president, Germany's Markus Brunnermeier is expected to become chief economist and France's Laurence Boone has reportedly been tapped to head the Markets Portfolio, a package deal that Christian Kopf of Union Investment said balances representation from northern and southern European countries. Kopf called de Cos the candidate with the "strongest technical understanding of monetary policy and central banking," adding that his appointment would signal Europe's commitment to price stability and a hard currency amid global assaults on central bank independence.

De Cos takes over at a time of resurgent inflation: euro area inflation rose to 4% in October, its highest level in more than three years, driven by energy costs from the Iran war. He will also inherit major projects including plans for a digital euro and long-delayed capital-markets integration. Lagarde recently warned that each year without capital markets integration means "more of our savings are invested abroad and more of our growing firms look elsewhere for funding." The ECB's Financial Stability Review this month flagged mounting risks from European investors' growing exposure to the U.S. economy and vulnerabilities to AI, while Lagarde told the European Banking Congress that her biggest concern was "AI applied together with cyber threat."

A core challenge for de Cos will be managing monetary policy for 21 economies growing at different speeds, a problem made urgent by France's potential debt crisis. French borrowing costs have risen as investors worry about its mounting public debt-to-GDP ratio, high budget deficit and contracting economy, compounded by political uncertainty ahead of France's presidential election in April. The ECB Executive Board has discussed what measures could be taken to prevent market disorder, though Ken Egan of KBRA said sovereign spreads have pulled back and market liquidity has improved in recent weeks, adding that "we are some way from having a serious conversation about ECB intervention." De Cos will also face a difficult policy balance: preventing higher energy costs from spreading into wages and wider prices while avoiding unnecessary damage to growth.

stories.headline: Dow erases 1,100-point loss in volatile session; S&P 500 and Nasdaq end lower but well off lows
stories.byline: Financial & Markets desk · anchored on Reuters
body: The Dow Jones Industrial Average erased an intraday loss of more than 1,100 points on Wednesday, closing 164.25 points higher, or 0.33%, at 50,182.95, in a dramatic reversal that traders attributed to light holiday trading and a bullish blog post by investor Michael Burry. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite also staged sharp comebacks but finished in negative territory: the S&P 500 fell 0.25% to 7,182.78, and the Nasdaq dropped 0.62% to 23,585.80. At their session lows, the Dow had lost 2.2%, the S&P 500 3.2%, and the Nasdaq 4.6%.

The rebound was fueled in part by the circulation of a blog post in which Burry said his portfolio is "temporarily almost entirely long," and by reduced trading volumes ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday. The Dow was lifted by gains in International Business Machines, Salesforce, and Sherwin-Williams, while S&P 500 sectors including materials, energy, and real estate all rose. However, AI-related stocks continued to decline: Nvidia dropped nearly 4%, Micron Technology fell 4.5%, Oracle lost more than 5%, and Alphabet shed over 2%. The State Street Technology Select Sector ETF (XLK) ended nearly 1% lower. Semiconductor maker Ambarella plunged more than 19% after reporting a light current-quarter forecast and missing third-quarter earnings and revenue estimates.

David Wagner, head of equities at Aptus Capital Advisors, described the market as "very bifurcated" between AI and non-AI stocks. "The market is pulling back obviously due to a pullback in tech, pullback in semis, pullback in the AI narrative, but right now, I don't see that being a growth scare. I see it being a sentiment-based scare" tied to factors such as the composition of Congress in the new year. He added that there remains a "big worry" that AI concerns could shift from sentiment to a growth scare "if the market starts pricing in too much Fed activity of hiking rates."

Investor sentiment was weighed by several macroeconomic headwinds. October's personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index showed headline inflation rising 0.3% month over month, putting the annual rate at 3.8%, up from 3.7% in September. Core PCE, excluding food and energy, increased 3.3% year over year, slightly above the Dow Jones forecast. The data reinforced expectations for interest rate hikes from the Federal Reserve in December and January, according to reports. The White House also unveiled new tariffs on more than a dozen major trading partners, including China and the European Union, adding to the risk-off mood.

Wednesday's volatile session followed a losing day for the S&P 500 and Nasdaq on Tuesday, when tech stocks gave back gains as Nvidia sank and Anthropic fell below its IPO price. The choppy trading is the latest in a month marked by sharp swings, including the ouster and reinstatement of Nvidia's Jensen Huang and the Democrats' sweep in the midterm elections, as investors debate the future of the AI build-out against a worsening macroeconomic outlook. U.S. stock markets will be closed Thursday for Thanksgiving and will close at 1 p.m. ET on Friday. Dow Jones futures rose modestly Thursday afternoon, along with S&P 500 and Nasdaq futures, as global markets showed signs of stabilization.

stories.headline: Semiconductor exports surpass oil and gas for first time in 2026 amid AI boom
body: Semiconductor exports have overtaken oil and gas in global trade value for the first time, according to a Deutsche Bank analysis of International Trade Centre data, driven by insatiable demand for artificial intelligence components. During the January-March quarter of 2026, four-quarter rolling totals for semiconductor exports reached about $1.61 trillion, compared with $1.53 trillion for oil and gas. The gap widened in the second quarter, with semiconductor exports totaling about $1.60 trillion and oil and gas exports reaching about $1.47 trillion.

The milestone arrives amid extreme volatility in semiconductor stocks. Last week, before a sharp reversal on Monday, the PHLX Semiconductor Index (SOX) suffered its worst weekly loss in a quarter century, plunging nearly 11% last Friday alone and capping a more than 17% weekly decline. Nvidia, the leading maker of artificial intelligence chips, soared more than 31% Monday after falling for seven consecutive weeks and plunging 46% during that stretch, then dropped almost 10% on Tuesday and Wednesday. Advanced Micro Devices tumbled 20% in two days last Thursday and Friday, and Micron Technology sank 27% over the seven days ended last Friday.

The shift reflects booming data center construction and hundreds of billions of dollars in orders for graphics processing units aimed at providing AI computing power, according to a Rothschild & Co. Redburn report last Thursday. 'Compute will be the new commodity fueling this transformation on a global scale,' said Rothschild analyst Cara Thomson. Disruptions to oil supplies through the Strait of Hormuz after the Iran war helped widen the gap between the two sectors: daily oil flows through the Strait collapsed nearly 77%, to 4.9 million barrels in the second quarter of 2026 from 21.6 million barrels in the fourth quarter of 2025, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

The changing dynamics in global trade carry macroeconomic implications similar to the explosion of oil trade in the 1970s. Oil-exporting countries historically recycled much of their surpluses into U.S. Treasuries and other bonds, helping finance U.S. deficits. Jim Reid, global head of macro and thematic research at Deutsche Bank, said that since semiconductor-surplus countries in Asia are more closely tied to U.S. tech companies, some chip-export earnings could flow back into U.S. technology stocks, startups and data centers, further financing the AI investment cycle. 'For decades we've talked about the petrodollar. Perhaps increasingly we need to think about the chip dollar,' Reid wrote in a report this month. He added that the shift could tilt the mix of global financial flows, potentially producing 'more growth, more excitement, more volatility, and structurally higher yields' in corporate and government debt.

stories.headline: U.S. tariff-hike threats pile pressure on partners, raising inflation and rate-hike risks
body: The Trump administration on Nov. 25 proposed new tariffs targeting 14 major trading partners, including China, the European Union, Vietnam, India, South Korea, Taiwan, Switzerland, and Singapore, as part of a strategy to curb excess industrial capacity and pressure countries to conclude trade deals with Washington. The proposed rates start at 15% for the EU, South Korea, Switzerland, and Taiwan and rise to as much as 35% for Vietnam, with China facing a capped rate of 20% on top of an existing 25% tariff. The U.S. Trade Representative's Office said it intends to cap the new duties at lower levels for countries that have completed trade deals or are still negotiating, giving some nations a strong incentive to speed up talks.

China faces a potential doubling of tariffs to 40% if the trade truce reached in South Korea last October is not extended beyond January, according to the USTR. Beijing has rejected Washington's claims of excess capacity, with Commerce Ministry spokesperson He Yadong calling on the U.S. to "rectify its wrongdoing and return to the right track of resolving issues through dialogue." Wendy Cutler of the Asia Society Policy Institute said Beijing "seems prepared to live with the new rates provided that they don't exceed 20%," and noted that Washington is using the tariffs as leverage to secure shipments of critical minerals and agricultural goods. Analysts said the proposal appears aimed squarely at China, with the word appearing hundreds of times in USTR reports on other countries.

India and Vietnam face proposed tariffs of 25% and 35%, respectively, but those rates could fall to 17% and 20% if ongoing talks produce reciprocal trade agreements. Vietnam's trade ministry said Thursday it was working to complete a deal as soon as possible. Singapore faces a maximum potential rate of 20%, which could fall to 10% with an agreement; its Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry said it was "very disappointed" and argued the proposal failed to account for the structure of its economy. Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong said about 33% of direct exports would be affected, and that the effective tariff rate would rise to 10.3% from 7.8% under the highest levy, adding, "I'm also very surprised that this has happened because this is not something that you would expect from an important major trading partner."

Exemptions for semiconductors and other electronics should cushion the impact on South Korea and Taiwan, analysts said. Taiwan's effective tariff rate would rise to about 9% from 6%. Switzerland, which negotiated a deal in November 2025 that slashed U.S. duties to 15%, now faces an additional 15% tariff from a new Section 301 investigation; its Economy Ministry said it rejected the allegations and assumed the latest recommendation was consistent with the earlier deal. The European Union rejected the finding that Europe was a source of industrial overcapacity, with Commission spokesperson Olof Gill saying the EU expects any measures to respect the existing 15% ceiling on EU goods. EU trade ministers are due to speak with USTR Jamieson Greer on Monday.

The proposed tariffs threaten to complicate the Federal Reserve's fight against inflation, which could hurt the stock market. Research from the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis indicates that tariffs contributed 0.5 percentage points to headline inflation as of June 2026. stories.headline: MLB sues players' union, asks court to declare lockout legal
body: Major League Baseball filed a lawsuit Wednesday against the MLB Players Association in federal court in the Southern District of New York, asking a judge to declare that a lockout would be legal and to prevent the union from dissolving its status as the players' bargaining representative. The legal action comes days before the current collective bargaining agreement is set to expire Monday night, after which the league and its 30 team owners are expected to lock players out of team facilities and cut off contact with team officials.

The league described the suit as a defensive measure. MLB spokesperson Glen Caplin said, 'Today’s filing is a defensive measure simply intended to keep the parties at the bargaining table to work towards a new collective bargaining agreement and a full 2027 season.' Caplin added that the league believes the union is preparing to 'disclaim' its status as the players’ representative in order to pursue an antitrust lawsuit, calling that a 'nuclear option' that would threaten MLB's antitrust exemption. 'We have asked a federal court in the Southern District of New York to proactively disarm the Union’s nuclear option of disclaiming,' Caplin said.

The players' union responded sharply, calling the lawsuit 'completely frivolous.' In a statement, the MLBPA said, 'We will respond appropriately, but MLB's decision to run to court in the middle of negotiations rather than bargain in good faith is incredibly disappointing.' The union has not threatened to dissolve or disclaimed its status, and the two sides remain in negotiations, though fundamental disagreements persist over the financial structure of the sport.

At the center of the dispute is a proposal from ownership to implement a salary cap and floor system, which the union has refused to consider. The league contends the union is stonewalling and threatening antitrust litigation to force MLB to abandon the cap proposal. The players have proposed increasing revenue sharing from higher-income teams to lower-income teams as an alternative, arguing that the cap proposal is designed to increase owners' profits and franchise valuations rather than improve competitive balance. The league has largely ignored that suggestion, according to the union.

The lockout, if it proceeds, would jeopardize the start of the 2027 season. The league has said it cannot sit idly by while the union's tactics threaten a full season, while the union blames ownership for demanding a fundamental restructuring of the game. With the CBA expiration imminent and negotiations showing little sign of resolution, the lawsuit adds a new layer of tension to the already contentious labor situation.

stories.headline: Steelers owner Art Rooney II backs Mike McCarthy, calls Aaron Rodgers insubordinate after release
body: Pittsburgh Steelers president Art Rooney II publicly backed head coach Mike McCarthy on Thursday, calling quarterback Aaron Rodgers insubordinate and saying his recent actions could not be tolerated. Rooney's comments came a day after Rodgers was released by the team following a 35-minute interview on ESPN's "The Pat McAfee Show" in which he berated McCarthy and accused him of sleeping through team meetings and skipping walk-throughs. Rodgers had been benched earlier in the week after giving McCarthy an ultimatum: relinquish play-calling duties or release him.

"I just want to say that I have 100% confidence in Mike McCarthy and I expect he'll be our coach this season, next season and beyond," Rooney told the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette. "The big thing, what happened this week, is insubordination can't be tolerated in any organization. When you start getting ultimatums, you can't live with that." Rooney also said Rodgers was "not a good teammate" and criticized the timing of his public comments, noting the Steelers are days away from a game against the Denver Broncos. "There's maybe a time and place after the season if he wanted to kind of unload," Rooney said. "He talks about wanting to be a good teammate, but you don't do that to your teammates a couple days before the game, that's for sure."

Rooney revealed that McCarthy had taken blame for some of the team's offensive struggles to protect Rodgers. "The sad thing is Mike took some of the bullets for Aaron in terms of some of the plays that were called, particularly in the red-zone troubles that we had," Rooney said. "Mike took some of the bullets for things that were going wrong down there. He tried to protect him, and it just wasn't working." One possible example cited was late in the first half of Pittsburgh's Week 8 win over the Browns, when the Steelers called three straight passing plays inside Cleveland's 10-yard-line despite running effectively. McCarthy accepted blame for those calls afterward.

Rooney expressed optimism that backup Mason Rudolph can lead the offense. Rudolph, a nine-year veteran with 20 career starts, delivered for the Steelers in a similar spot in 2023. Asked if he regretted bringing Rodgers back, Rooney said he was disappointed with how things turned out. "We certainly had hopes that he would be successful here, and I thought at times we certainly got on a roll," he said. "We had high expectations. It's easy to say, knowing what I know today, what would I do? But we had a good experience last year, and so I kind of wasn't expecting it to go this way this year."

The Steelers are scheduled to host the Denver Broncos on Friday at 3:00 p.m. ET. Despite the team's last two ugly losses and some sources corroborating Rodgers' claims about McCarthy, Rooney said he expects McCarthy to remain the coach "this season, next season and beyond."

stories.headline: LeBron James becomes oldest NBA player to record a triple-double as 76ers top Heat
body: LeBron James became the oldest player in NBA history to record a triple-double, posting 25 points, 12 assists and 10 rebounds to lead the Philadelphia 76ers to a 111-104 victory over the Miami Heat in an NBA Cup group-stage game on Wednesday night in Philadelphia. James, who turns 42 on Dec. 30, broke his own age mark for a triple-double at 41 years and 330 days old. The win improved the 76ers to an Eastern Conference-best 15-4 and snapped Miami's seven-game winning streak, dropping the Heat to 10-7.

James scored a season-high 25 points, including a stretch of 14 consecutive points in the second quarter that turned a three-point deficit into a 62-53 halftime lead. He shot 4 of 6 from three-point range, highlighted by a 35-foot pull-up three. Tyrese Maxey led all scorers with 30 points for Philadelphia, and rookie VJ Edgecombe added 18 points. Giannis Antetokounmpo led Miami with 32 points and 14 rebounds. The 76ers played without Joel Embiid (illness) and lost Jaylen Brown to a hamstring injury late in the first half.

James now has 126 career triple-doubles, a total that exceeds the combined career triple-doubles of Larry Bird, Michael Jordan, Kobe Bryant and Scottie Pippen, according to the Associated Press. He also connected on a halfcourt lob to Edgecombe for a layup early in the fourth quarter and later set up forward Dominick Barlow for an alley-oop dunk. "That's my favourite aspect of my game besides my IQ," James said of setting up teammates. "To be able to go out there and just play like a quarterback role and watch these guys run the right routes, and it's my job to put it on time and on target, it was fun."

Heat coach Erik Spoelstra, who coached James during Miami's back-to-back championships in 2012 and 2013, said before the game: "Father Time always wins. But right now, he's giving Father Time hell." James addressed his ability to step up when the team needs him most: "If they need me to dust off the cape from time to time, I can still accomplish that."

Both teams are now 2-1 in East Group B of the NBA Cup. Miami would have clinched the group with a win. The idle Dallas Mavericks became the first team to reach the Cup knockout round, clinching West Group A when the Phoenix Suns lost 116-104 at Houston. In that game, Kevin Durant became the fifth player in NBA history to score 33,000 points, joining James, Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, Karl Malone and Kobe Bryant. Houston's Alperen Şengün recorded his 15th career triple-double with 23 points, 11 rebounds and 11 assists, passing Hakeem Olajuwon for the second-most triple-doubles in franchise history.

In other NBA Cup action, the Minnesota Timberwolves remained unbeaten in Cup competition at 3-0 with a 113-106 win over the Oklahoma City Thunder. Jaden McDaniels had 32 points, 10 rebounds and 5 assists, becoming the third player in Timberwolves history to log at least 30 points, 10 rebounds and 5 assists in consecutive games, joining Karl-Anthony Towns and Kevin Garnett. The defending NBA and NBA Cup champion New York Knicks beat the Cleveland Cavaliers 121-102 for their sixth straight win. At Portland, the Trail Blazers defeated the San Antonio Spurs 116-111, leaving West Group C with four teams tied at 2-1. Spurs star Victor Wembanyama scored 44 points and grabbed 16 rebounds in the loss.

stories.headline: Kevin Durant becomes fifth player in NBA history to reach 33,000 points
body: Kevin Durant made NBA history Wednesday night, becoming the fifth player in league history to reach 33,000 career points. Durant, playing for the Phoenix Suns, entered the game against the Houston Rockets needing 14 points and crossed the milestone with a three-pointer with 46.3 seconds remaining in the second quarter. He finished with 20 points in the Suns' 116-104 NBA Cup loss in Houston.

Durant joins Kobe Bryant, Karl Malone, Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, and LeBron James in the exclusive 33,000-point club. "It's cool," Durant told reporters after the game. "I try not to make it about myself in there. I understand that it's rare to hit these type of accomplishments and I don't ever want to undersell it, but we're playing a team game and it's not about me most of the time." He added that he appreciates teammates who take time to celebrate individual achievements, noting that the Suns also celebrated Rockets center Alperen Sengun's triple-double that night.

The milestone came amid a heated exchange between Durant and Rockets guard Dillon Brooks in the final minute of the game. With roughly 30 seconds left in the fourth quarter, the two players stopped playing and went nose-to-nose near halfcourt while play continued around them. Both players received double technical fouls, and Brooks was ejected with 23.8 seconds remaining after picking up his second technical.

Durant addressed the exchange in his postgame comments. "I just love basketball. That's simple. I love to play ball. I love everything about the game, all the details that add up to winning," he said. "I don't mind if somebody got a grievance with me. I don't mind addressing it right there in the moment. I'm sure I said some things that he probably didn't like and he addressed it right there. And I can respect that as a man. And it didn't get farther than that. But if it does get farther than that, I'll be ready for that, too."

Durant and Brooks have a history of on-court clashes, which intensified after they were swapped for one another in a blockbuster trade between Phoenix and Houston last year. Earlier this month, tensions flared again when Brooks took subtle shots at Durant's former tenure in Phoenix following an online back-and-forth between Durant and Suns owner Mat Ishbia.

stories.headline: Neuralink Receives FDA Approval to Launch Pivotal Brain Implant Trial for ALS Patients
body: Neuralink has received approval from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to launch the LINK Pivotal Study, the first pivotal trial for an implantable brain-computer interface (BCI) in the United States. The company announced the development on November 25, stating that the study will evaluate the safety and effectiveness of its BCI system in individuals with severe paralysis due to amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Enrollment is now open, and the trial is expected to expand across multiple clinical sites in the U.S.

The LINK Pivotal Study builds on findings from Neuralink’s ongoing early feasibility studies in the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom, where over 30 implanted participants have collectively contributed thousands of hours of real-world BCI use. Participants have used their Neuralink implants to pursue higher education, express creativity, play video games, communicate with loved ones, and more. The study will evaluate the ability of participants to control digital devices through thought, focusing on functional outcomes that improve independence in daily life, while also assessing the system’s long-term safety and reliability.

The system being evaluated uses Neuralink’s N1 Implant, which records neural activity through fine electrode threads placed in the brain’s motor cortex, the region associated with movement. The implant detects electrical signals associated with intended movements and translates them into commands that allow users to interact with digital devices. Participants can learn to move a computer cursor by imagining moving their hand, without physically moving their limbs. The implant is inserted using the company’s R1 surgical robot, which places the fine electrode threads into the brain. The N1 device sits within the skull, with no external wires or battery pack, and communicates wirelessly with a computer, charging wirelessly through the scalp.

Neuralink’s existing Telepathy programme has demonstrated cursor navigation and mouse functions, including left, right and middle clicks. Participants have also used the technology for activities such as messaging, browsing the internet, writing code, creating digital artwork, and playing video games. The company’s clinical-trial information says participants undergo surgery under general anesthesia, and the published study pathway includes health screening, brain imaging, implantation, device training, and follow-up assessments extending to 24 months after implantation.

The new study represents a move beyond Neuralink’s earlier-stage human testing. Its PRIME programme was designed as an early feasibility study to evaluate the initial safety and functionality of the N1 Implant, R1 Robot, and associated software in people with paralysis. A pivotal trial is a later-stage clinical investigation intended to generate evidence about a medical device’s safety and effectiveness for a specific intended use, which can support a subsequent regulatory application, although successful completion does not guarantee marketing authorization. The FDA’s approval to launch LINK does not mean the Neuralink implant has been approved for general medical use; the company continues to describe its devices as investigational and available only through authorized clinical research.

Neuralink hit a milestone last year when the company revealed that its first participant with ALS, named Bradford Smith, was able to communicate using brain signals alone. “Neuralink has given me freedom, hope, and faster communication. ... It has improved my life so much. I'm so happy to be involved in something big that will help many people,” Smith said at the time. The company’s announcement did not disclose the planned number of participants or provide a detailed breakdown of clinical sites. The milestone could bring Neuralink closer to establishing the clinical evidence needed for a future regulatory submission, but the pivotal study will need to demonstrate that the implant can provide reliable digital-device control while maintaining an acceptable safety profile over an extended period.

stories.headline: Public health risks from lead plume after Iowa munitions detonation
body: When the U.S. Army destroyed its stockpile of lead azide on Wednesday at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, residents felt the blast from a mile away. Linda Ross, who lives near the facility, described hearing the explosion and feeling things rattle on her window panes, calling the event 'a little anticlimactic.' FEMA has characterized the containment effort as one of the most complex mitigation efforts in history.

The Environmental Protection Agency has stated that lead leaks were not detected in the air, but public health experts caution that the full picture may take weeks or months to emerge. Will Sander, an associate professor of preventive medicine and public health at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, told NPR that while the air statement may hold, 'we may still find additional detections, particularly as you start doing more testing in the soil and water around the area.' He noted that many mitigation measures were implemented only after a legal challenge and public outcry, and that the groundswell 'certainly helped move the needle forward and provide more mitigation in place.'

Sander advised residents to remain cautious even after the shelter-in-place order was lifted. He recommended looking for any dust or accumulation of materials and washing it off, as suggested before the blast, and paying close attention to test results in the coming days. Asked if he would return immediately if he lived there, Sander said he would 'want to stay away a little bit longer until I got some more confirmatory testing that everything was all clear.' For those who must go back, he suggested staying inside for another day or so and wearing a mask if going outside, adding that after the next 24 hours he would be less worried about inhaling airborne material.

Weather conditions, including rain or snow, could help wash material off hard surfaces, Sander said, though he acknowledged that lead will get into the dirt regardless. He noted that background lead contamination already exists in soil and that the blast is unlikely to 'markedly increase that even if there was lead from this blast.' When asked about long-term risk assessment, Sander said it is 'still way too early' and that monitoring should continue for weeks to potentially months to ensure no long-term impacts. He predicted there would be 'a lot of lessons learned' from how the situation was approached and communicated, as well as for future efforts to mitigate similar materials stored across the country.

stories.headline: Astronomers may have discovered a primordial black hole formed before the first stars
body: Astronomers may have identified a primordial black hole, a relic from the earliest moments of the universe, after detecting a mysterious object that briefly magnified a distant star. The object, named Phoebe, was observed on December 18, 2019, when a star in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a satellite galaxy of the Milky Way, gradually brightened for about an hour before returning to normal. The smooth, symmetrical change in brightness, with no explosion or flare, matched the pattern of gravitational microlensing, a phenomenon predicted by Einstein's general theory of relativity in which an invisible object's gravity bends and magnifies the light of a more distant star.

Researchers at Swinburne University in Melbourne identified the signal while reviewing observations from a survey that frequently monitored stars in the Large Magellanic Cloud. The distinctive pattern convinced the team they had detected a genuine gravitational microlensing event, but the nature of the invisible object remained uncertain. Three possibilities were considered: a rogue planet expelled from its original solar system and traveling through the Milky Way; a similar wandering planet located within the Large Magellanic Cloud, which would make it the first planet discovered through microlensing beyond our galaxy; or a primordial black hole, an ancient object formed in the first fractions of a second after the Big Bang, long before the first stars appeared.

The unusually short duration of the brightening—approximately 60 minutes—provided a key clue to Phoebe's mass. Using models of the event, researchers estimated the object has a mass roughly three times that of the Moon, far smaller than any planet in our solar system and well below the threshold for a conventional black hole formed by a collapsing star, which typically has a mass at least five times that of the Sun. If Phoebe is a black hole, its tiny mass would point to a primordial origin rather than stellar collapse.

To investigate where Phoebe might belong, the researchers compared the likelihood that the object originated from different populations, including stars in the Milky Way, stars in the Large Magellanic Cloud, and objects associated with the surrounding dark matter halo. The results strongly favored the dark matter halo, with the team's calculations indicating Phoebe is approximately 100,000 times more likely to belong to this population than to one associated with ordinary stellar matter. While this does not confirm that Phoebe is a primordial black hole, it makes a potential connection to dark matter particularly intriguing.

If the primordial black hole interpretation is correct, Phoebe could be among the oldest objects ever detected, having formed before the first atoms and stars existed, when the universe was still experiencing the extreme conditions that followed the Big Bang. For roughly 13 billion years, such an object could have traveled unseen through space until its gravity briefly magnified the light of a distant star on a single night in December 2019, offering astronomers a remarkable glimpse of something born near the very beginning of the universe. The findings were published in a paper on arXiv on May 19, 2026, by a team including researchers from Swinburne University and other institutions.

stories.headline: Engineered molecular glue stabilizes chromosomes in aging eggs, raising hopes for IVF improvement
body: Researchers at the Max Planck Institute for Multidisciplinary Sciences in Göttingen, Germany, have engineered a novel protein system that restores normal chromosome connections in aging mouse eggs, according to a study published Thursday in Science. The system, called TALhesins, is designed to act as a molecular glue that tethers chromosomes together, counteracting the loss of a natural protein complex called cohesin that deteriorates over time. In experiments with eggs from older mice, TALhesin reduced premature chromosome separation, increasing the proportion of eggs with properly connected chromatids from 47% to 74% — a level comparable to that seen in young mice.

The work addresses a phenomenon known as aneuploidy, the leading cause of age-related infertility, failed IVF cycles, and miscarriage. Aneuploidy occurs when chromosomes fail to separate correctly during egg cell division, and it rises dramatically around age 40: studies show that between 50% and 80% of embryos from women in their 40s carry chromosomal abnormalities. The underlying driver is the gradual loss of cohesin, a ring-like protein that holds sister chromatids together. Unlike most cells, where cohesin works for only hours before being cleaved, in oocytes it must maintain bonds for decades — from before birth until fertilization triggers the final stages of meiosis.

Melina Schuh, a director at the Max Planck Institute who led the research, said her lab has already begun adapting TALhesin to bind to chromosomes in human eggs. “We have initial signs that there is a positive effect on cohesion,” she told STAT, but cautioned that the team has not yet tested whether the system can reduce errors in human oocytes. Rajiv McCoy, a biologist at Johns Hopkins University not involved in the work, called the proof of concept “highly successful,” noting that technologies that reduce aneuploidy could expand women’s biological reproductive windows and reduce miscarriage rates. “The stakes are very high,” he said.

The TALhesin proteins are designed to attach to specific DNA regions near the centers of each chromosome and include a deactivation switch based on cohesin’s natural cleavage sites, so they automatically release chromosomes only when fertilization occurs. Eva Hoffman, a molecular geneticist at the University of Copenhagen who was not involved in the study, said the findings challenge the conventional view that aneuploidy is irreversible. “Since cohesion is established during fetal life and has to be maintained for decades, its depletion over time was thought to be irreversible,” she said. She stressed that clinical potential depends on safety studies for embryonic development.

Schuh has co-founded a startup, Ovo Labs, based in Munich and London, that has licensed TALhesin from the Max Planck Institute and is working to commercialize the technology. A key hurdle is that most eggs retrieved in IVF have already undergone the first meiotic division, meaning cohesin loss may have already caused errors that cannot be fixed. Retrieving and treating immature eggs could prevent some errors but requires maturation in lab dishes, which is not widely used and has drawbacks. Schuh is hopeful they can establish a system to treat oocytes earlier in meiosis. Ovo Labs faces competition from U.K.-based U-Ploid, co-founded by Schuh’s colleague Alexandre Webster, which is developing a different approach called Lyvanta. At the 2026 meeting of the American Society for Reproductive Medicine, U-Ploid reported that 65.5% of treated immature eggs matured without detectable chromosome errors, compared to 35.7% of untreated eggs, though the eggs were not fertilized and Lyvanta has not yet been tested in patients or shown to improve pregnancy rates.

Currently, for older women struggling to get pregnant, the only widely available solution is repeated IVF cycles, which are expensive and inefficient. For women between 35 and 40, the odds of getting pregnant are about one in three IVF cycles; for women over 40, it drops to one in ten. Some clinics offer experimental add-ons with shaky scientific backing, and a recent STAT investigation found that hundreds of women in their late 30s and 40s have traveled to clinics in Ukraine, Albania, and elsewhere seeking mitochondrial replacement techniques to boost IVF odds, despite scant evidence it can overcome aneuploidy. Schuh’s team plans to continue testing TALhesin in human eggs, with the long-term goal of developing a treatment that could reduce aneuploidy in eggs used for IVF.

stories.headline: FCC authorizes SpaceX to deploy up to 1 million satellites for orbital data center project
body: The Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday granted SpaceX conditional authorization to deploy a constellation of up to 1 million satellites designed to serve as orbital data centers. If fully deployed, the constellation—called Starmind—would increase the number of satellites in orbit by roughly 50-fold. The decision, announced a day before the Thanksgiving holiday, represents a major regulatory victory for SpaceX and its founder, Elon Musk, who has allied himself with the Trump administration.

The FCC authorization gives SpaceX a long deployment runway: seven years to launch its first operational Starmind satellite, until November 2035 to deploy 100,000 operational satellites, and until November 2040 to deploy the full constellation. SpaceX has proposed operating the satellites in six orbits ranging from 550 km to about 1,000 km. The Starmind satellites would primarily communicate using lasers to connect with other satellites, including SpaceX’s Starlink, and the FCC’s approval gives SpaceX the authority to use radiofrequency communications to maintain contact and control from Earth if primary systems fail.

The approval is conditional and does not establish that orbital data centers are technically or economically viable. SpaceX faces significant challenges, including dramatically reducing the cost of manufacturing and launching satellites, cooling processors in space, and securing financing for chips destined for orbit. The FCC has not yet approved SpaceX’s plans for handling orbital debris for satellites operating above 600 km. SpaceX requested a waiver of existing FCC rules that require satellites ending missions below 2,000 km to reenter Earth’s atmosphere within five years; the company wants the flexibility to move retired satellites into other Earth orbits or heliocentric orbits around the Sun.

The FCC granted the authorization despite objections from Amazon, Viasat, and the American Astronomical Society, which flagged concerns over orbital debris and congestion, radiofrequency interference, and environmental consequences. Amazon, which is building a competitor to SpaceX’s Starlink service, argued in its petition that the application lacked basic details and described it as a “lofty ambition rather than a real plan,” while also warning that the proposal “risks real harm.” The FCC dismissed some key concerns, including potential threats to scientific research, because the agency determined they fell outside its regulatory authority.

FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement: “The United States is moving decisively to ensure that this breakthrough technology creates opportunity, drives investment, and delivers lasting benefits for the American people. This action opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth.” Musk thanked Carr in a post on X, writing, “Much appreciate. This will be a great asset to America and the world.” The initial regulatory approval does not mean orbital data centers are imminent; SpaceX must still clear other regulatory hurdles and resolve technical and economic questions before deployment can proceed.

stories.headline: Nvidia faces governance crisis after Jensen Huang reinstated as CEO amid code-of-conduct violations
body: S&P Global Ratings is considering downgrading Nvidia’s credit rating, citing governance concerns and “key man risk” following the ouster and reinstatement of CEO Jensen Huang, who admitted to violating the company’s code of conduct. The agency expects to complete its review within 90 days and could cut Nvidia’s rating from AA to AA-, the fourth-highest on its scale. Although Nvidia would retain its investment-grade status, a downgrade could raise its borrowing costs and ripple through the AI infrastructure loans it guarantees.

Huang addressed the code-of-conduct violation during his first all-hands meeting after returning as CEO, emphasizing that no one is exempt from the rules but that violations do not automatically lead to termination. “Facts, circumstances, a lot of assessments” still matter, he said, according to Wired. The admission has created an awkward cultural risk: employees may feel embarrassed or angry about working for a company where the CEO broke the rules without facing consequences, ethics experts warn.

Matt Plass, chief market strategy officer at LRN, a compliance training firm, said that for many workers, ethics are paramount. “They’re really embarrassed and angry when senior leadership lets them down,” he told TechCrunch. Plass noted that companies typically remove an executive after an investigation and then launch a “hearts-and-minds initiative” to rebuild trust. But that playbook is harder at Nvidia, where Huang is seen as nearly inseparable from the company’s success and no clear succession plan exists.

The governance concerns extend beyond culture. S&P cited “weak executive oversight and lack of succession planning” as reasons for the potential downgrade. In August, Nvidia announced plans to arrange $500 billion in financing for AI infrastructure with six financial institutions, including Goldman Sachs, Apollo, and Blackstone, with Nvidia guaranteeing 25% of the loans. Even before Huang’s ouster, lenders had been demanding larger guarantees, Bloomberg reported. A downgrade would likely intensify those demands, raising costs for neoclouds and other infrastructure companies that rely on Nvidia’s backing.

Despite the turmoil, an employee campaign for Huang’s reinstatement suggests morale has not yet suffered. However, as pressure mounts in the coming months, sidestepping the code of conduct could cost Nvidia something harder to measure: its employees’ pride in the company. Plass acknowledged that for firms where the CEO is a “godhead figure,” dealing with such infractions is “much, much harder.”
